entries.a9f885862de53597ad4cc900de0afd8bb25e892e: <div sID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="1Chr.18" sID="1Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7831" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> David's piety and his prayer we had an account of in the foregoing chapter; here follows immediately that which one might reasonably expect, an account of his prosperity; for those that seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof, as David did, shall have other things added to them as far as God sees good for them. Here is, I. His prosperity abroad. He conquered the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">ver. 1</reference>), the Moabites (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.2">ver. 2</reference>), the king of Zobah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3-1Chr.18.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), the Syrians (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.5-1Chr.18.8">ver. 5-8</reference>), made the king of Hamath his tributary (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.9-1Chr.18.11">ver. 9-11</reference>), and the Edomites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.12-1Chr.18.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. II. His prosperity at home. His court and kingdom flourished, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.14-1Chr.18.17">ver. 14-17</reference>. All this we had an account of before, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1-2Sam.8.18">2 Sam. viii.</reference>
entries.9014310861176f00d2e8beb2efed2904aa7ff1d3: <div eID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7831" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Victories. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1042.)</title> <div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them, and took Gath and her towns out of the hand of the Philistines. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he smote Moab; and the Moabites became David's servants, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought gifts. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. <hi type="super">4</hi> And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot <hi type="italic">horses,</hi> but reserved of them a hundred chariots. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then David put <hi type="italic">garrisons</hi> in Syria-damascus; and the Syrians became David's servants, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought gifts. Thus the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserved David whithersoever he went. <hi type="super">7</hi> And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">8</hi> Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. <div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">After this,</hi> it is said (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">v. 1</reference>), David did those great exploits. After the sweet communion he had had with God by the word and prayer, as mentioned in the foregoing chapter, he went on his work with extraordinary vigour and courage, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer.</hi> Thus Jacob, after his vision, lifted up his feet, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1">Gen. xxix. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> We have taken a view of these victories before, and shall now only observe, 1. Those that have been long enemies to the Israel of God will be brought down at last. The Philistines had, for several generations, been vexatious to Israel, but now <hi type="italic">David subdued them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">v. 1</reference>. Thus shall all opposing <hi type="italic">rule, principality, and power,</hi> be, at the end of time, put down by the Son of David, and the most inveterate enemies shall fall before him. 2. Such is the uncertainty of this world that frequently men lose their wealth and power when they think to confirm it. Hadarezer was smitten <hi type="italic">as he went to establish his dominion,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">v. 3</reference>. 3. <hi type="italic">A horse is a vain thing for safety,</hi> so David said (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">Ps. xxxiii. 17</reference>), and it seems he believed what he said, for he <hi type="italic">houghed the chariot-horses,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">v. 4</reference>. Being resolved not to trust to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>), he would not use them. 4. The enemies of God's church are often made to ruin themselves by helping one another, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.5">v. 5</reference>. The Syrians of Damascus were smitten when they came to help Hadarezer. When hand thus joins in hand they shall not only not go unpunished, but thereby they shall be gathered <hi type="italic">as the sheaves into the floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. 5. The <hi type="italic">wealth of the sinner</hi> sometimes proves to have been <hi type="italic">laid up for the just.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Syrians brought gifts,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.6">v. 6</reference>. Their shields of gold and their brass were brought to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.7-1Chr.18.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. As the tabernacle was built of the spoils of the Egyptians, so the temple of the spoils of other Gentile nations, a happy presage of the interest the Gentiles should have in the gospel church.
entries.df578fb2c098977b75a53f57f798cd03c8c24406: <div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; <hi type="super">10</hi> He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou;) and <hi type="italic">with him</hi> all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass. <hi type="super">11</hi> Them also king David dedicated unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with the silver and the gold that he brought from all <hi type="italic">these</hi> nations; from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. <hi type="super">12</hi> Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he put garrisons in Edom; and all the Edomites became David's servants. Thus the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserved David whithersoever he went. <hi type="super">14</hi> So David reigned over all Israel, and executed judgment and justice among all his people. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Joab the son of Zeruiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, recorder. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, <hi type="italic">were</hi> the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; <hi type="super">17</hi> And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David <hi type="italic">were</hi> chief about the king. <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7837" type="x-p"/> Here let us learn, 1. That it is our interest to make those our friends who have the presence of God with them. The king of Hamath, hearing of David's great success, sent to congratulate him and to court his favour with a noble present, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.9-1Chr.18.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. It is in vain to contend with the Son of David. <hi type="italic">Kiss the Son,</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">lest he be angry;</hi> let the kings and judges of the earth, and all inferior people too, be thus wise, thus instructed. The presents we are to bring him are not <hi type="italic">vessels of gold and silver,</hi> as here (those shall be welcomed to him who have no such presents to bring), but our hearts and sincere affections, our whole selves, we must present to him as living sacrifices. 2. That what God blesses us with we must honour him with. The presents of his friends, as well as the spoils of his enemies, <hi type="italic">David dedicated unto the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.11">v. 11</reference>), that is, he laid them up towards the building and enriching of the temple. That is most truly and most comfortably our own which we have consecrated unto the Lord, and which we use for his glory. Let our <hi type="italic">merchandise and our hire be holiness to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa. xxiii. 18</reference>. 3. That those who take God along with them whithersoever they go may expect to prosper, and be preserved, whithersoever they go. It was said before (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.6">v. 6</reference>) and here it is repeated (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.13">v. 13</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went.</hi> Those are always under the eye of God that have God always in their eye. 4. God gives men power, not that they may look great with it, but that they may do good with it. When David reigned over all Israel he <hi type="italic">executed judgment and justice among all his people,</hi> and so answered the end of his elevation. He was not so intent on his conquests abroad as to neglect the administration of justice at home. Herein he served the purposes of the kingdom of providence, and of that God who <hi type="italic">sits in the throne judging right;</hi> and he was an eminent type of the Messiah, the <hi type="italic">sceptre of whose kingdom is a right sceptre.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen7837" type="x-p"/>

entries.4381c6590667f5e61f3724a02df95f6258e2e37c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3803"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen5452" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference>, 2. David Subdues the Philistines and Moabites.<div eID="gen5452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3803"/><hi type="bold">1. David ... took Gath and her towns--</hi>The full extent of David's conquests in the Philistine territory is here distinctly stated, whereas in the parallel passage (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference>) it was only described in a general way. Gath was the "Metheg-ammah," or "arm-bridle," as it is there called--either from its supremacy as the capital over the other Philistine towns, or because, in the capture of that important place and its dependencies, he obtained the complete control of his restless neighbors. <div eID="gen5453" type="x-p"/>
entries.aade43229f98358df4c8fa05cfc6d241db653610: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3804"/><div sID="gen5454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3804"/><hi type="bold">2. he smote Moab--</hi>The terrible severities by which David's conquest of that people was marked, and the probable reason of their being subjected to such a dreadful retribution, are narrated (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen5454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Moabites ... brought gifts--</hi>that is, became tributary to Israel.<div eID="gen5455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5456" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3-1Chr.18.17">1Ch 18:3-17</reference>. David Smites Hadadezer and the Syrians. <div eID="gen5456" type="x-p"/>
entries.d767908901e7460071cd6ce6e89707b00b0c25c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3805"/><div sID="gen5457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3805"/><hi type="bold">3. Hadarezer--</hi>or, "Hadadezer" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>), which was probably the original form of the name, was derived from Hadad, a Syrian deity. It seems to have become the official and hereditary title of the rulers of that kingdom.<div eID="gen5457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zobah--</hi>Its situation is determined by the words "unto" or "towards Hamath," a little to the northeast of Damascus, and is supposed by some to be the same place as in earlier times was called Hobah (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.15">Ge 14:15</reference>). Previous to the rise of Damascus, Zobah was the capital of the kingdom which held supremacy among the petty states of Syria.<div eID="gen5458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates--</hi>Some refer this to David, who was seeking to extend his possessions in one direction towards a point bordering on the Euphrates, in accordance with the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Ge 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>). But others are of opinion that, as David's name is mentioned (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Ch 18:4</reference>), this reference is most applicable to Hadadezer. <div eID="gen5459" type="x-p"/>
entries.efac6f8effbb319bbc156c83a3e09528d2cea007: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3806"/><div sID="gen5460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3806"/><hi type="bold">4-8. And David took from him a thousand chariots--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3-2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:3-14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference> David is said to have taken seven hundred horsemen, whereas here it is said that he took seven thousand. This great discrepancy in the text of the two narratives seems to have originated with a transcriber in confounding the two Hebrew letters which indicate the numbers, and in neglecting to mark or obscure the points over one of them. We have no means of ascertaining whether seven hundred or seven thousand be the more correct. Probably the former should be adopted [Davidson's HERMENUTICS].<div eID="gen5460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but reserved of them an hundred chariots--</hi>probably to grace a triumphal procession on his return to Jerusalem, and after using them in that way, destroy them like the rest. <div eID="gen5461" type="x-p"/>
entries.e974313ff5c0b5d70979746c3a7d3302e79b800d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3808"/><div sID="gen5463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3808"/><hi type="bold">9-13. Tou--</hi>or Toi--whose dominions border on those of Hadadezer. (See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9-2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.15">1Ki 11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen5463" type="x-p"/>
entries.f43a7cee7e0e6b4fb26162e589a560fde5008501: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3809"/><div sID="gen5464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3809"/><hi type="bold">17. the Cherethites and the Pelethites--</hi>who formed the royal bodyguard. The Cherethites were, most probably, those brave men who all along accompanied David while among the Philistines, and from that people derived their name (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sa 30:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.16">Eze 25:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">Zep 2:5</reference>) as well as their skill in archery--while the Pelethites were those who joined him at Ziklag, took their name from Pelet, the chief man in the company (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.3">1Ch 12:3</reference>), and, being Benjamites, were expert in the use of the sling. <chapter eID="1Chr.18"/>

entries.4b131e741795e91a099b1bc75bb807a587088141: <div eID="gen13673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13674" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13674" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> David smites the Philistines, and takes Gath, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Chr 18:1</reference>. Reduces the Moabites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.2">1Chr 18:2</reference>. Vanquishes Hadarezer, king of Zobah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Chr 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Chr 18:4</reference>. Overcomes the Syrians of Damascus, and takes several of their cities, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.5-1Chr.18.8">1Chr 18:5-8</reference>. Tou, king of Hamath, congratulates him on his victory, and sends him vessels of silver, gold, and brass, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.9">1Chr 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.10">1Chr 18:10</reference>. Those and the different spoils he had taken from the conquered nations, he dedicates to God, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.11">1Chr 18:11</reference>. Abishai defeats the Edomites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.12">1Chr 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.13">1Chr 18:13</reference>. David reigns over all Israel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.14">1Chr 18:14</reference>. His officers, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.15-1Chr.18.17">1Chr 18:15-17</reference>. <div eID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> David - took Gath and her towns - See the comparison between this chapter and <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sam 8:1</reference> (note), etc., in the notes on the latter.
entries.1dcb8a229654cd783b248623e9958a031c3e643e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> Brought gifts - Were laid under tribute.
entries.62c2e6fe55deef79288b2d99202a5d814b2b7fc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> Tou king of Hamath - Called Toi in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9">2Sam 8:9</reference>.
entries.740544a5360546a6711b80fc3a5bd7620a772f39: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> Abishai - slew of the Edomites - This victory is attributed to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sam 8:13</reference>. He sent Abishai against them, and he defeated them: this is with great propriety attributed to David as commander-in-chief; qui facit per alterum, facit per se.
entries.19bd8d8e44be81b6e5ccbf58f9a0e7e54b583cd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> Joab - was over the host - General-in-chief. <div eID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat - recorder - The king's remembrancer, or historiographer royal.
entries.ec267014657a304b3f7e9a0d33e356b8b55c1073: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> Zadok - and Abimelech - priests - Both high priests; one at Gibeon, and the other at Jerusalem, as we have seen <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Chr 16:39</reference>. <div eID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> Shavsha was scribe - Called Seraiah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sam 8:17</reference>.
entries.ac96d82ee4d2a4d5b8f771a47499c6446d435db0: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> Cherethites and the Pelethites - See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sam 8:18</reference>. <div eID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> The Targum says, "Benaiah was over the great Sanhedrin and the small Sanhedrin, and consulted Urim and Thummim. And at his command the archers and slingers went to battle." <div eID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13688" type="x-p"/> The sons of David - These were the highest in authority.  <chapter eID="1Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen13688" type="x-p"/>

entries.b9d6e0de83074133fb49d0e12c8b42242c719c20: <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1-1Chr.18.17">1Ch 18:1-17</reference> <div eID="gen5800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5801" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in these three chapters are all narrated in the second book of Samuel also, and in the same order. First, there are grouped together in our 18th chapter, and in 2 Sam 8, in such a manner as to afford a general view of the whole, all the wars which David carried on victoriously against all his enemies round about in the establishment of the Israelitish rule, with a short statement of the results, followed by a catalogue of David’s chief public officials. In 1 Chron 19 and in 2 Sam 10 we have a more detailed account of the arduous war against the Ammonites and Syrians, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:1-3</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:26-31</reference> the conclusion of the war with the capture of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites; and finally, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4-1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:4-8</reference>, we have a few short accounts of the victories of the Israelitish heroes over giants from the land of the Philistines, which are inserted in <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.18-2Sam.21.22">2Sa 21:18-22</reference> as a supplement to the last section of David’s history. Apart from this last section, which is to be regarded even in the Chronicle as an appendix, we find the arrangement and succession of the events to be the same in both books, since the sections which in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:1-13</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1-2Sam.11.12">2Sa 11:1-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.25">2Sa 11:25</reference>, stand between the histories of the wars, contain sketches of David’s family life, which the author of the Chronicle has, in accordance with his plan, omitted. Even as to individual details the two narratives are perfectly agreed, the divergences being inconsiderable; and even these, in so far as they are original, and are not results of careless copying, - as, for instance, the omission of the word נציבים,   <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.6">1Ch 18:6</reference>, as compared with <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.13">1Ch 18:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>, and the difference in the numbers and names in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Ch 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.8">1Ch 18:8</reference>, as compared with <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.8">2Sa 4:8</reference>, are, - partly mere explanations of obscure expressions, partly small additions or abridgments. For the commentary, therefore, we may refer to the remarks on 2nd Samuel, where the divergences of the Chronicle from the record in Samuel are also dealt with. With <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1-1Chr.18.13">1Ch 18:1-13</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1-2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:1-14</reference>; and with the register of public officials, <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.14-2Sam.18.17">2Sa 18:14-17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:15</reference>-18. <div eID="gen5801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5802" type="x-p"/> Examples of paraphrastic explanation are found in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference>, where the figurative expression, David took the bridle of the mother out of the hands of the Philistines, i.e., deprived them of the hegemony, is explained by the phrase, David took Gath and her cities out of the hands of the Philistines, i.e., took from the Philistines the capital with her daughter cities; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.17">1Ch 18:17</reference>, כּהנים is rendered by, the first at the king’s hand. Among the abridgments, the omission of David’s harsh treatment of the Moabites who were taken prisoners is surprising, no reason for it being discoverable; for the assertion that the chronicler has purposely omitted it in order to free David from the charge of such barbarous conduct, is disposed of by the fact that he does not pass over in silence the similar treatment of the conquered inhabitants of Rabbah in 1Ch 20:3. Instead of this, the chronicler has several historical notes peculiar to himself, which are wanting in the text of Samuel, and which prove that the author of the Chronicle has not derived his account from the second book of Samuel. Such, e.g., is the statement in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.8">1Ch 18:8</reference>, that Solomon caused the brazen sea and the pillars and vessels of the court of the temple to be made of the brass taken as booty in the war against Hadadezer; in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.11">1Ch 18:11</reference>, the word מאדום, which is wanting in Samuel, as מארם, which in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.11">1Ch 18:11</reference> of that book is used in place of it, probably stood originally in the Chronicle also. Such also are the more accurate statements in <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.12">1Ch 18:12</reference> as to the victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sa 8:13</reference>).  <chapter eID="1Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen5802" type="x-p"/>
